tosafot:a1.1: Rather, isn’t it referring to one witness, and it teaches that when he does not contradict him he is deemed credible; learn from it: but if he contradicts him, [the witness] is not believed. And it must mean that he said “I do not know,” for had he said outright “I did not eat,” it is obvious that he is exempt, since one witness stands only for an oath, as I explained in the mishna.
rashi:a3.1: A person is deemed credible about himself: in matters that involve atonement, he would not hold back from bringing a sin offering to gain atonement before his Maker.
gershom:a1.1: [A printer’s marker: up to here belongs to 11b.] What is the reasoning of the Rabbis, who exempt him?
gershom:a2.1: Because a person is credible about himself: in a matter that involves neither liability to death, nor liability to lashes, nor liability to pay money, but only an obligation of atonement, and he says that he does not need it, he is believed more than a hundred witnesses.
rashi:a3.2: Since if he wishes, etc.: had he wanted to lie, he could have said, “I was acting intentionally”; and what he said, “I did not eat,” means “I did not eat unwittingly, but intentionally.”
tosafot:a3.1: In brief: At first glance, the Gemara means that he is believed by force of a miggo, since he could have said “I was intentional.” Tosafot find this difficult on two counts. First, it is a miggo against witnesses, since witnesses say that he ate and he says “I did not eat,” and Bava Metzia 81b rules that we do not say miggo against witnesses (the case of “do not go by way of the river Pakod, go by way of Naresh”). Second, it is no miggo at all, since a person does not make himself wicked, as in the case in Kiddushin 50a, where the Gemara suggests that one spoke to exempt himself from an offering, answers that he would then have said “I was intentional,” and objects that a person does not make himself wicked. Tosafot answer that he is believed here because his statement can be explained: when he said “I did not eat,” he can mean “I did not eat unwittingly, but intentionally,” and that is what the Gemara’s miggo means: since he could have said “I was intentional” and been exempt, we read his “I did not eat” as meaning this, since that was his intent. And although a person does not make himself wicked (Sanhedrin 9b, “so-and-so sodomized me”), that is only to disqualify himself; but if he says “I ate forbidden fat intentionally,” he is believed, since he means well: he does not want to bring a non-sacred animal into the Temple courtyard. If you ask, let us ask him whether that was his intent: even if he later says “not unwittingly but intentionally,” since he did not say so at the time, Rabbi Meir holds him liable. So it is in the Torat Kohanim: Rabbi Meir says, if at the outset he says “I was intentional,” we listen to him; but if he argued with them all day, saying “I did not eat,” and said no more, then even if he afterward says “not unwittingly but intentionally,” he is liable. If you ask how Rabbi Meir can hold him liable when he says “I did not eat,” since he will not bring a sin offering against his will, as Bava Kamma 40a says that one does not take a pledge from those liable for sin offerings: there it is where he says that he does not want atonement; this one does want atonement, but thinks he is exempt, so a pledge is taken from him. gershom:a3.1: Or perhaps they exempt him because one can say miggo.
rashi:a4.1: For impurity: for example, they said to him, “You became impure and immediately came into the Temple.”
tosafot:a4.1: The difference is to resolve from it the case of impurity: and it could equally have said that the difference is where he said “I did not eat, neither unwittingly nor intentionally.”
gershom:a4.1: To resolve from it the case of impurity: if they said to him, “You became impure and entered the Temple, and you are liable to an offering,” and he says, “I did not become impure.”
gershom:a5.1: Even with impurity a person is believed and exempt, no matter whether it is new impurity, where they tell him, “You became impure today and today you entered the Temple,” or old impurity, where they tell him, “You became impure yesterday and today you entered the Temple”: when he says “I did not become impure,” he is exempt, since a person is credible about himself.
rashi:a5.1: Old impurity: “Yesterday you became impure, and today you entered.”
gershom:a6.1: And if you say that the reason the Rabbis exempt him is that we say miggo, then it is when they exempt him, etc.
rashi:a5.2: New impurity: there is no miggo of “I immersed,” since he cannot say that, for they told him, “You entered at the time of your impurity”; and even if you immersed, your sun had not set, and a tevul yom [one who has immersed but whose sun has not yet set] who enters the Temple unwittingly is liable to a sin offering, as is said in Menaḥot, in the chapter HaKometz Rabba (Menaḥot 27b): one who lacks atonement and entered the Temple is liable to a sin offering, and all the more so a tevul yom. Nor can one say [the miggo of] “intentionally,” since we require that his statement be explicable: had he said to them, “I did not enter,” his statement could be explained as “I did not enter unwittingly, but intentionally”; but since he said to them, “I did not become impure,” even if he means “I did not become impure unwittingly, but intentionally,” he is not exempt from the offering, for with the impurity we do not care whether it was unwitting or intentional, since the entry into the Temple was unwitting.
tosafot:a5.1: In brief: “I did not remain in my impurity”: according to Rabbi Meir, although his statement can be explained, he is not believed, since it is a “why would he lie” against witnesses. As for what is said in several places, that all agree we do not say miggo against witnesses, that is where their testimony is complete, as Tosafot explained in Ḥezkat HaBatim: “This one says, ‘It was my ancestors’…,” where Rava said “why would he lie, if he wished he could say ‘I bought it from you’,” and Abaye said that we do not say miggo against witnesses; there his statement could be explained too (“my ancestors” meaning “as good as my ancestors,” since I rely on them), but there the witnesses are complete. So too where one who says “I did not borrow” is treated as one who says “I did not repay,” and is not believed where witnesses said that he borrowed: why not, since we hold that one who lends before witnesses need not be repaid before witnesses, let him be believed when he says “I did not borrow,” meaning “I did not remain in the loan, but repaid”? Rather, there the witnesses completed their testimony. But the Riva [Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Asher] says that we do not believe him against witnesses to cause his fellow a loss even where his statement can be explained, only here, to exempt him from an offering so that he not bring a non-sacred animal into the courtyard; and this settles the case in Ḥezkat HaBatim. It seems that the Rabbis disagree only where he says “I did not eat,” but if he said “I ate shuman [permitted fat],” they concede to him [Rabbi Meir], and so it is implied in the Tosefta. But this makes the passage above difficult, where it says that the practical difference is to resolve the case of impurity: why not say it is one who says “I ate shuman,” where explaining his statement does not apply, giving a difference within the case of forbidden fat itself? gershom:a7.1: But for new impurity he is liable, since miggo cannot be said, for the witnesses tell him: “You became impure just now, did not immerse, and entered the Temple now.” What [then]? [A printer’s note: it seems it should read: “And Rabbi Meir told them that the a fortiori argument is better and primary, etc.”] (Obvious, etc. He told them that the a fortiori argument is better and primary, even though there is a miggo.)
rashi:a7.1: You became impure: and you came into the Temple.
rashi:a7.2: Exempt: as is said below: “that he shall confess”: one who admits the matter is liable; one who does not admit the matter is exempt.
rashi:a8.1: Actually, the Rabbis’ reasoning is because of miggo: and it is in old impurity that they disagree. And we read: “And this is what it is teaching.”
gershom:a8.1: And this is what it is teaching: since, if he wished, he could have told him, “I became impure” [and then immersed].
gershom:a9.1: It is dealing with old impurity, where miggo can be said, as was said above: since if he wished he could say “I immersed” and be exempt, when he says “I did not become impure” too, etc. Therefore a person is credible about himself.
rashi:a8.2: If so: if regarding impurity they disagree on this, that Rabbi Meir does not accept miggo and the Rabbis accept miggo, this is the same as the forbidden fat of our mishna, and why do I need both?
gershom:a10.1: If so: what does it teach us? This baraita is the same as forbidden fat: since they hold that we say miggo, we could learn it from “they said to him: You ate forbidden fat.”
rashi:a9.1: “I ate fat”: the Rabbis accept miggo there because his statement can be explained, etc.; but with impurity, where one cannot say “I did not become impure unwittingly, but intentionally,” I might say that his statement cannot be explained. It teaches us that it can be explained in another way: “I did not remain in my impurity.”
gershom:a11.1: Even so, this baraita was necessary. Lest you say that it is with “I ate forbidden fat” that his statement can be explained, so as to say miggo: since he could say “I did not eat unwittingly, but intentionally,” when he says “I did not eat” he is also exempt.
gershom:a12.1: But [where] he says, “I did not become impure,” his statement cannot be explained as “I did not become impure unwittingly, but intentionally,” since even if he became impure intentionally he is impure, and when he entered the Temple unwittingly he is liable. [It teaches us that] here too the statement can be explained, so as to say miggo: since if he wished he could say “I immersed,” what he means by “I did not become impure” is also “I did not remain in impurity, but immersed.”
rashi:a10.1: “That he shall confess”: “that in which he has sinned”: written in Leviticus with regard to the impurity of the Temple.
gershom:a13.1: “That he shall confess”: “that in which he has sinned,” which is written with regard to hearing the voice [of an oath] and the impurity of the Temple and its sacred foods.
gershom:a14.1: One who admits the matter: who does not contradict the witnesses, is liable.
gershom:a15.1: This “Rabbi Yehuda says” is the same as the Rabbis of the mishna, who disagree with Rabbi Meir.
rashi:a12.1: The Sages concede to Rabbi Yehuda: and they disagree with Rabbi Meir regarding fats, for example, “You ate forbidden fat,” and he says, “I did not eat”; and regarding entering the Temple, they said to him, “You entered the Temple impure,” and he says, “I did not enter.”
gershom:a16.1: And the Sages concede: other Sages, and not those of the mishna.
gershom:a17.1: To Rabbi Yehuda: who is the same as the Rabbis of the mishna.
gershom:a18.1: With regard to fats: [where they said to him,] “You ate forbidden fat.”
gershom:a19.1: And with regard to entering the Temple: that a person is credible about himself. If two said to him, “You became impure and entered the Temple,” and he says, “I did not enter” [meaning] not unwittingly but intentionally, he is exempt from the offering, since he does not contradict the witnesses by [saying] that he did not become impure; rather, he became impure and entered intentionally.
gershom:b6.1: Another version: they say that this “And the Sages concede” refers to the Rabbis of the mishna. But with impurity they do not concede to him.
rashi:a12.2: But with impurity: for example, where he said “I did not become impure,” they do not concede to him, and do not hold that he is exempt. Evidently, the Rabbis’ reason is miggo, that his statement can be explained, as in “I did not act unwittingly, but intentionally”; but with “I did not become impure,” where this cannot be said, they do not concede to Rabbi Yehuda. And the dilemma is resolved: the reason is miggo, and nothing more.
tosafot:a12.1: In brief: Rashi explained this in two versions, and the Ri explained another approach. “And the Sages concede to Rabbi Yehuda… but with impurity they do not concede to him”: as in “You became impure,” and he said, “I did not become impure.” The Gemara asks: in what case? If old impurity, what is the difference between this case and that one? Rather, learn from it that it is new impurity, and that is why they do not concede, since miggo does not apply: the Rabbis’ reason is miggo, and they concede only with fats and with forbidden relations, where miggo applies, but not with impurity, where it does not; whereas Rabbi Yehuda, whose reason is that a person is credible about himself, exempts in both. So the dilemma is resolved: the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Meir reason from explaining his statement, as is implied here, whereas if the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Meir were Rabbi Yehuda, the reason would be that a person is credible about himself. Ravina rejects this: actually, it is old impurity, meaning that nothing is proven from here, since we can say that even Rabbi Yehuda believes him only by miggo. Where they disagree here in old impurity and the Rabbis hold him liable, it is where witnesses say, “You ate sacred food in bodily impurity,” and he said, “I did not become impure”: the Rabbis do not consider that his statement can be explained as meaning “I did not remain in my impurity, but immersed.” Had he said “I did not eat,” we could explain his statement as “I did not remain in my impurity, but immersed first”; but when he says “I did not become impure,” his first miggo is already contradicted with regard to the impurity of contact, since “I did not become impure” implies neither unwittingly nor intentionally, as he did not answer them about the eating, which is what they had said to him. Tosafot then find this passage difficult against the first chapter of Bava Metzia (3b), which says “let his own admission not be greater than the testimony of witnesses” by an a fortiori argument, and objects: “What of his own mouth, which renders him liable to an offering, as opposed to witnesses, who do not render him liable to an offering?” What is the objection? His mouth renders him liable to an offering only when witnesses do not contradict him: if he says “I ate forbidden fat unwittingly,” and witnesses testify that on that day and at that hour they warned him, or that it was shuman, he is not liable on [the strength of his mouth]; and with witnesses whom his mouth does not contradict, he is liable, even with one witness, as is implied here. Moreover, on the contrary, witnesses are more stringent than his mouth, since they render him liable even when his mouth contradicts them, for the Rabbis exempt him only because of miggo, while if he contradicts them outright he is liable to an offering. And further, what does Rabbi Ḥiyya answer there, that he holds like Rabbi Meir? Even according to the Rabbis they render him liable where his statement cannot be explained. gershom:a20.1: But with impurity: if the witnesses said to him, “You became impure,” and he said, “I did not become impure,” they do not concede to him that he is believed.
gershom:a21.1: What are we dealing with: in which impurity do they not concede to him?
gershom:b7.1: [In the other version:] What are we dealing with: in which impurity do they not concede to him? If we say old impurity, what is different about fats and entering the Temple, etc.
gershom:b1.1: [A printer’s marker: up to here belongs to 12a.] If we say old impurity, what is different about fats and entering the Temple, where, as we said, they concede to him that he is believed, since miggo can be said and he does not contradict them, for if he wished he could say “I was intentional”?
gershom:b2.1: With old impurity, too, his statement can be explained, since miggo can be said: if he wished he could say, “I did not remain, etc.” Rather, it must be that in new impurity they do not concede to him, since miggo cannot be said; and learn from it that the Rabbis’ reason is miggo.
gershom:b8.1: [In the other version:] Rather, isn’t it with new impurity that they do not concede to him? And Rabbi Yehuda holds that even with new impurity a person is believed.
rashi:b2.1: Ravina said: Actually: the reason is miggo. With fats and entering the Temple there is the miggo “I did not enter unwittingly, but intentionally”; and regarding impurity they do not concede to him because there is no miggo; and although an offering applies to it and it is old impurity, there is old impurity that has no miggo, for example where they said to him, “You ate sacred food, etc.”
gershom:b3.1: Ravina said: Actually, it is in old impurity that they do not concede to him, for in new impurity even Rabbi Yehuda himself would not hold that he is credible about himself, since miggo cannot be said, and all the more so the Sages would not hold that he is believed.
gershom:b4.1: Rather, in what case does it say “but with impurity they do not concede to him”? It is said even of old impurity: “Yesterday [you became impure] and today you ate sacred food.” And with old impurity like this they do not concede to him, since it has no miggo: for example, where witnesses said to him, “You ate sacred food in impurity, since you had become impure,” for which he is liable to an offering if unwitting and to karet if intentional, and he said, “I did not become impure.” Here his statement cannot be explained by a miggo without contradiction, and he cannot say, “I did not remain in impurity, but immersed.”
gershom:b9.1: [In the other version:] Ravina said: Actually, old impurity. That is: what forces you to establish it as new impurity, where they do not concede to him because it has no miggo? Even with old impurity you can say that they do not concede to him, and you find a case of it with no miggo, like this: where the witnesses said to him, “You ate sacred food,” as was said above. And my teacher told us that the first version is more reasonable.
rashi:b2.2: [Rashi now gives another version of the passage from 12a on:] Another version: The Sages concede to Rabbi Yehuda with fats and entering the Temple, which involve an offering; but with mere impurity, without entering the Temple, where there is no offering, they do not concede to him.
rashi:b2.3: With impurity: and he touched pure items.
rashi:b2.4: And what are we dealing with? If old impurity, etc.: rather, since it states without distinction that they do not concede to him with any impurity, learn from it that the reason is not miggo, for with old impurity there is a miggo; rather, the reason is that a person is credible about himself. Therefore, where there is an offering, it is so, but with mere impurity, it is not.
rashi:b2.5: And the Gemara asks: what impurity are we dealing with, where there is no miggo? If old impurity, there is a miggo, so why do they not concede to him with old impurity?
rashi:b2.6: Ravina said: Actually: there is old impurity that has no miggo, for example where they said to him, “You became impure yesterday and ate sacred food today,” which is bodily impurity, and you are liable to a sin offering; and he says, “I did not become impure,” contradicting them both about the eating and about the touching, [meaning] that he neither ate nor touched sacred food in impurity. And if he now goes back and says, “When I said ‘I did not become impure,’ I meant ‘I did not remain in impurity’,” he intends only to exempt himself from the offering: regarding the eating, which carries an offering, he contradicts them; regarding the touching, he does not contradict them; and his first statement is contradicted with regard to the impurity of contact.
gershom:b5.1: For what would he say to them? If he says to them, “I immersed and ate,” when he says this to them, his first statement is contradicted with regard to the impurity of contact, in that he touched impurity. For when he said “I did not become impure,” that means he did not become impure at all, and when he then says “I immersed,” it implies that he became impure; so his first statement, “I did not become impure,” is contradicted. And why can his statement not be explained here, as in the case where they said to him “You became impure” with old impurity and he said “I did not become impure”? Because that is not comparable to this: here he does not answer them about what they said to him. They tell him, “You ate sacred food in bodily impurity,” and he does not answer “I did not eat,” but says “I did not become impure,” which means “I did not become impure [at all],” so here his statement cannot be explained, as we said. Therefore, with old impurity like this they do not concede to him. And Rabbi Yehuda holds that even in this case he is believed, since his statement can be explained as “I did not remain in my impurity,” and actually the reason is miggo.
gershom:b10.1: Rav Naḥman said that Rav said: the halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, that a person is credible about himself. [The daf’s text reads only: Rav Naḥman says.]
rashi:b4.1: He did not say: Rabbi Yehuda did not say that he is believed and pure, except to eat pure items by himself; but he should not eat in front of others, lest they come to treat pure items lightly.
rashi:b4.2: With regard to himself: he is believed to eat the pure items that he touches, since a person is credible about himself; but he may not feed them to others.
gershom:b11.1: He did not say it: Rabbi Yehuda did not say that a person is credible about himself except by himself and with regard to himself. That is, although he is believed that he did not become impure, he may not eat sacred food in public, only in private, by himself, and with regard to himself, and not [the food] of others.
gershom:b12.1: Another version: with regard to himself, he may eat [lit. “feed”], since he himself knows that he did not become impure; but not others, lest they come to say that everywhere a person is credible about himself more than one hundred witnesses.
rashi:b5.1: Rabbi Meir concedes, etc.: but the miggo of the mishna he does not accept, since it is easier for him to lie and say “I did not eat” than to make himself wicked and say it was intentional.
tosafot:b5.1: Since if he wished he could say, “I did not complete the act of intercourse”: for the witnesses do not testify that they saw the whole act; but with forbidden fat they saw the whole act, only they did not know what was in his heart. And with the nazirite, too, although they saw the whole act, it is possible that he was never bound [by the prohibition], unlike forbidden fat, by which he is bound. And with regard to testimony, it is possible that he was not one bound to “tell” [Leviticus 5:1], since he did not intend to testify, and the verse states: “and he is a witness.”
gershom:b13.1: And Rabbi Meir concedes to the Sages: that he is credible about himself, where two said to him, “You had intercourse with an espoused maidservant, etc.”
gershom:b14.1: Since if he wished he could say, “I did not complete my act of intercourse”: for he is liable only with emission of semen, and that is not clear to the witnesses, so their testimony is no testimony; therefore he is believed to say, “I did not have intercourse.” And likewise with the nazirite to whom they said, “You became impure through a corpse and you are liable to an offering”: since, if he wished, he could tell them, “You thought that I was a nazirite at that time, but I was not, for I had already requested release from my naziriteship before a Sage,” or “there was a condition in my heart and the condition was not fulfilled,” so the testimony is no testimony; therefore he is believed.
rashi:b6.1: I requested: from a Sage, regarding my vow, and I became impure when it was permitted; and this is what I meant: “I did not become impure while still under my vow.”
rashi:b7.1: You know testimony: and he had him take an oath, and he did not admit, and [they say] you are liable to the offering for the oath of testimony: [he is exempt] by a miggo, since he could exempt himself in a permitted way and say, “What did I mean by ‘I do not know’? I meant that I did not intend to be a witness.”
tosafot:b7.1: I had not intended to testify: from here my teacher said, and so ruled in practice, that witnesses who heard a matter from the parties themselves but did not intend to testify, and were not brought there for any testimony, their testimony is worthless if they come later to testify before a court.
gershom:b15.1: And likewise when they said to him, “You know testimony for so-and-so, for you saw the event, as we saw that you were there, and if you do not testify for him you are liable to an offering for ‘hearing the voice of an oath’,” and he said, “I do not know,” he is exempt, since, if he wished, he could tell them, “I did not intend testimony; I did not set my mind to remember or not.” Therefore their testimony is no testimony, and he is believed.
rashi:b8.1: Fat and fat: two olive-bulks of forbidden fat.
gershom:b16.1: He ate fat and fat: he ate an olive-bulk of forbidden fat and again ate an olive-bulk in one lapse of awareness; since it is one name, fat, he is liable only one sin offering. But if he ate an olive-bulk of fat and an olive-bulk of blood, notar and piggul in one lapse of awareness, since they are many types, even though it is in one lapse of awareness, he is liable for each and every one.
gershom:b19.1: Abaye said to him: this is the reason that he is liable two: lapses divide, and there are two lapses.
gershom:b17.1: And a stringency with one type: that two half olive-bulks combine to render him liable.
gershom:b18.1: From two types: one olive-bulk [from two types], exempt, since they do not combine.
rashi:b12.1: From one type, liable: this refers to the latter clause of the mishna, which teaches: two half olive-bulks from one type, liable. Obvious!
tosafot:b12.1: Where he ate them in two dishes: and the first clause, “he ate fat and fat,” is established as one dish, and “fat, piggul and notar” also in one dish: he is liable for each one, since they are three names. But it is puzzling: rather than distinguishing between fat and fat and fat, piggul and notar, let it distinguish within fat and fat itself, between one dish and two dishes. One can say: because it wanted to teach in the latter clause, “this is a stringency with one type, etc.” And as for what it teaches, “this is a stringency with many types, etc.,” that stringency is found with one type too, for example in two dishes; one can say that it means: a stringency with many types, that he is always liable for each one, whether in one dish or two dishes, excluding one type in one dish, where he is liable only one.
gershom:b20.1: For example, where he ate the olive-bulk in two dishes: cooked dishes, half an olive-bulk roasted and half an olive-bulk boiled.
gershom:b21.1: And according to Rabbi Yehoshua: it was necessary to say that he is liable, for he says in the mishna that dishes divide with regard to sin offerings, as we learned: “Rabbi Yehoshua said: I heard regarding one who eats, etc.”
rashi:b13.1: Lest you say that when Rabbi Yehoshua said: below in this chapter: dishes divide. [The printed Rashi has here, in parentheses, the words “two half olive-bulks from one type, liable.”]
rashi:b13.2: Whether for leniency: for example, he ate two half olive-bulks in two dishes: they do not combine.
rashi:b13.3: Or for stringency: that if he ate two olive-bulks in two dishes in one lapse of awareness, he is liable two. It teaches us that from one type he is liable, even in two dishes, and Rabbi Yehoshua does not disagree.
rashi:b13.4: It teaches us: that he said it for stringency.
gershom:b22.1: Lest you say: that when Rabbi Yehoshua said that dishes divide, there is no difference whether for leniency or for stringency. For in the mishna, where they divide so as to render him liable for each one, that is for stringency [the printed text adds here the word me’ila]; and here it would be a leniency, one olive-bulk in two dishes, for if you say that dishes divide, they do not combine to render him liable. The mishna teaches us “from one type, liable,” even in two dishes. Evidently Rabbi Yehoshua said that dishes divide for stringency, and not for leniency.
rashi:b14.1: This is the reading: “From two types, exempt. Obvious!” And since the latter clause, where they do not combine, deals with one type and two dishes, by inference the first clause, which teaches “from one type, liable,” that they combine, means one type and one dish. Obvious!
gershom:b23.1: From two types, exempt: obvious, since they do not combine.
gershom:b24.1: Reish Lakish said: this “from two types” is one type; and why does it call it two types? For example, where he ate it in two dishes. And it says that although it is one type, since he ate it in two dishes, dishes divide and they do not combine, and he is exempt; for he says that dishes divide no matter whether for leniency or for stringency.
tosafot:b17.1: From the latter clause, one type and two dishes, etc.: but above, where it established the first clause as one type and two dishes, it did not infer that the latter clause, “from two types,” is literally two types, for example forbidden fat and blood, since one can say that the tanna taught the latter clause on account of the first clause, but he would not teach the first clause on account of the latter clause.
gershom:b25.1: And from the latter clause, one type and two dishes, as we said: by inference the first clause, which teaches “from one type, liable,” is one type and one dish.
rashi:b18.1: There is no awareness for a half-measure: he ate half a measure and became aware: it is not an awareness that divides, so that if he again ate half a measure, they combine.
tosafot:b18.1: Who says there is no awareness for a half-measure: and it calls it one lapse of awareness according to Rabban Gamliel, who does not count awareness for a half-measure; and in any case it teaches it to inform us that even in one lapse of awareness, from two types he is exempt.
gershom:b26.1: Obvious that he is liable. Ravina said: What are we dealing with here? Where he had awareness in the interim: he became aware that he had eaten half an olive-bulk of forbidden fat, and again ate half an olive-bulk unwittingly. And it teaches us that although he had awareness in the interim, so that he did not eat them in one lapse of awareness, he is liable.
rashi:b19.1: One who writes two letters: this is a [complete act of] labor on Shabbat.
gershom:b27.1: And according to Rabban Gamliel, who says there is no awareness for a half-measure: that awareness he had in the interim, for a half-measure, is not counted as awareness to divide the measure, so that they would not combine and he would be exempt; rather, it is not awareness, and they combine, as we learned: “One who writes two letters on Shabbat,” for in this case he is liable [even] in two lapses of awareness, one in the morning and one in the evening, where he had awareness in the interim: Rabban Gamliel deems him liable, etc.
rashi:b21.1: Mishna. How much time can one who eats them expend: for the two half olive-bulks, which he said combine.
gershom:b28.1: How much time can one who eats an olive-bulk of forbidden fat, or an olive-bulk of blood, or an olive-bulk of notar expend: that is, how long may he draw out and extend his eating so that it still counts as eating and he is liable?
rashi:b21.2: As though he were eating toasted grain: they are measured as though they had been crumbled into fine crumbs, like toasted grain, and he eats them one by one; within the length of that delay, they combine.
gershom:b29.1: As though he were eating toasted grain: that is, even if he took an olive-bulk and broke it into crumbs, and took each crumb and ate it one after the other, like one who eats toasted grain kernel after kernel, nevertheless, since he finished and completed the olive-bulk, it is an act of eating and he is liable.
rashi:b21.3: Peras: explained in Eruvin (82b): a loaf of three to the kav, half of it for [the measure of] a house afflicted with leprosy. Half a loaf is a peras, from the word perusa [a slice], and it is four eggs[’-bulk].
tosafot:b21.1: From beginning to end, the time it takes to eat a half-loaf: from here it is implied that the measure of a peras applies in two ways. One is with regard to interruption: if he paused between one eating and the next for the length of a peras, it does not combine. The other is as we say elsewhere (Pesaḥim 44a): if he put an olive-bulk of teruma into a peras’ measure of non-sacred food and ate them, he is liable for it.
rashi:b22.1: He ate impure foods: his body is disqualified from teruma if he ate half a peras, as we say in Eruvin, in the chapter Keitzad Mishtatfin (82b): “and half of its half to disqualify the body.”
tosafot:b22.1: Impure foods, etc.: some books read “creeping creatures,” and it deals with impure ones. And if you ask, derive [his impurity] from when he touched them: one can say that his fellow thrust it into his throat.
rashi:b22.2: Entered the Temple: this refers back to the quarter-log of wine, since for impure foods he is not liable for entering the Temple.
rashi:b22.3: If he interrupted in it: that he did not drink the quarter-log of wine at once.
rashi:b23.1: Gemara. As a stringency: as though eating toasted grain one by one, close to one another; by that they measure, so that if he ate as much as half an olive-bulk and paused, and after that time ate another half olive-bulk, even if from beginning to end he took longer than the time it takes to eat a peras, [eating] close to one another, they combine, and even if that measure is the whole day.
gershom:b30.1: And the Rabbis say: this is the measure of eating for which he is liable: until he expends, from the start of eating the olive-bulk to its end, the time it takes to eat a half-loaf. Rabbi Meir says it as a stringency: even though he takes longer than the time it takes to eat a half-loaf, since he draws out his eating and does not interrupt in between, even if he draws it out the whole day, it is an act of eating and he is liable; that is the stringency. And the Rabbis say to him, etc.
rashi:b23.2: Or perhaps he says it as a leniency: for in this he holds like the Rabbis, that beyond the time it takes to eat a peras it does not combine; and that is why he compares it to toasted grain: if he did not pause in between, but [ate] as one eats toasted grain, which is eaten one right after another, it combines; and if he paused, it does not combine, even within the time it takes to eat a peras.
gershom:b31.1: Or perhaps he says it as a leniency: as though eating toasted grain one after another, that he not interrupt between them, and it also requires the time it takes to eat a half-loaf; but if he interrupted in between, then even though from beginning to end it is within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf, since he interrupted in between, he is exempt.
